utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Glad to you again, Mr. Siller. We both seem to have a very long day today. So, Mr. Siller, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Oric. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and distinguished gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution, and with me is Joanne Richardson as co-counsel, and also Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio. We have our and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence for Mr. Oric. We have with us here our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Before we admit the witness in the courtroom, are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have no preliminaries on this side. We would just like to announce that we did receive the Defence reply for the 94 bis, and that we're taking that under contemplation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We have received it too, and we've started working on it, together with the other filing. Just some housekeeping matters, information more or less, more than anything else. I should like to inform you that on Friday, the 11th of February, when we are scheduled to sit in the morning, we will be unable to sit because there is an extraordinary Plenary of the Judges taking place. And as I am the chair of the Rules Committee, there is no way I can escape my responsibilities there. So I have to be present throughout the entire sitting, session, of the Plenary, which I anticipate will take the entire morning at least, entire day most -- more probably. So there will be no sitting on the 11th, all right? Okay. Second piece of information I wanted to give you is that, next week we were scheduled to sit in the afternoon, with the exception of Friday. Through the hard work of my staff, we have succeeded in shifting all the sittings to the morning, bar Thursday, the 10th, bar Thursday the 10th. It's not because we have not succeeded in shifting it, but because as we were sitting in the afternoon, I had made a personal appointment which is -- which I cannot change now, because it doesn't depend on me, and I have to be at my appointment at round about 10.00, and I don't know how long that's going to take. So rather than trying to split the morning sitting in two parts, I would rather keep it in the afternoon, as it was originally scheduled. So on the 10th, we will be sitting in the afternoon and not in the morning, all right? Okay. Otherwise, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday we'll be sitting in the morning rather than -- instead of the afternoon. Does that cause you any problem, Ms. Richardson or Mr. Di Fazio, Ms. Sellers? It doesn't cause you any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: None at all, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither does it cause the Defence any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're still in time to shift, because all this was done in the last hours, you know, when it could be done. All right? Good. Any preliminaries on your parts? None? Where's the usher? There. Could you escort the witness in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gligic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you are receiving interpretation of what I'm saying in your own language, and that you can understand what is being said, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is the volume of your -- in your earphone, headphones, good enough? Do you want it higher or do you want it lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So good afternoon once more, and welcome to this Tribunal. You are soon going to start giving testimony in this case, which the Prosecution has instituted against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, in the sense that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn undertaking is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to give to you. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to welcome you and thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. Let my introduce myself. I'm the Presiding Judge in this trial. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. To my right is Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from Denmark, and to my left, Judge Albin Eser from Germany. Together we preside over this trial. You have been summoned here as a witness by the Office of the Prosecutor. But once here, occupying that chair where you're sitting now, you are a testimony -- you are a witness, you are a witness of this Tribunal, and you do not have the freedom or the liberty to consider yourself as the witness of the Prosecutor rather than the witness of the Defence, or consider yourself to be a witness against the accused. You are not a witness against the accused, you're just a witness, you're a witness of this Tribunal. As a result of this, as a consequence, you have a responsibility and a duty, pursuant to the oath that you have taken earlier on, to answer all questions, irrespective of who is putting the questions to you, whether it's the Prosecutor or the Defence, answer all questions, wherever they are coming from, as truthfully, as fully, and as honestly as possible. Do I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any problems with any question that may be put to you at any time, either by the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution or by the Defence, please draw our attention straightaway. We will listen to what you have to say and we will decide accordingly. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure is the Prosecution goes first, and I understand that Ms. Sellers will be putting -- examining you in the first place. She will then be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is appearing for Naser Oric. Whether you will be here again tomorrow or not, or how long you are going to stay -- be here giving evidence very much depends on how you answer. The shorter you keep your answers, the better it is. Please answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question, if you can. Sometimes witnesses have a tendency to tell us whole stories. We are not interested in what is not being asked from you or of you, so please try to restrict your answers, as much as possible, to the question that is put to you. And if it's a question that only requires you to answer yes or no, just answer yes or no. And this is for your own good. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'll ask permission again to lead the witness on background material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please go ahead. And unless I'm stopped by the Defence, it means that there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gligic. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Branislav Gligic. I was born in 1964, on the 7th of April, in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that the Skelani that was in the municipality of Srebrenica in the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, am I right in understanding that you have an identical twin brother, and that both of you have the same nickname, which is Pira?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And that your ethnic origin is that of Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In 1985, after completing high school, did you complete your compulsory military service, where you studied communications?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I served the military service in Skopje, in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you studied communications during that time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I did not study communications. I was merely trained in radio and telegraph and in establishing communication links between units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, after your military service, isn't it true that you were a toy salesman, and that you sold toys at the fairs and the local fetes in the Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And with your profession of selling toys, you travelled to several towns, and were quite familiar with the villages and hamlets that surrounded the Skelani town.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In 1992, were you living in Skelani with your mother, your father, and your twin brother?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you please confirm to the Trial Chamber that Skelani is a small town that sits on the banks of the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And that Skelani, in 1992, had about 400 households and about 1.200 residents.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Also, isn't it true that Skelani was basically an agricultural community, but that you also had people who raised livestock there?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, above the town of Skelani, are there villages, such as the village of Zabokvica?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are these villages that lie above the town of Skelani mainly Muslim towns or Serb towns?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Above Skelani, the place where I live, there are predominantly Serb villages, although there are some that are Muslim as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And from the town of Skelani, you can look up into the mountains behind the town and see these other villages; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Across from the town of Skelani, looking toward the Drina River, is there the city of Bajina Basta that's located in what is Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to tell the Trial Chamber, prior to 1992, what were your relationships with the Bosnian Muslims who lived in the Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: My relationship with my neighbours, Muslims, were excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you sell toys to both Muslims and to Serbs, and to any residents in those areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I frequented fairs, both those organised by the Muslims and the Serbs. There were religious festivities that I would use as an occasion to sell toys both to the Muslims and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, prior to April of 1992, did you notice any tensions that were starting to form between the Muslims and Serbs in the Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In the area in and around Skelani, in the villages that I frequented, in the end of 1989 and in 1990, tensions heightened. The SDA party was established and followed by the establishment of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, because of the tensions that arose, did you join one of the parties, the SDS party, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you join any political party?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My political party was a movement for Yugoslavia by Ante Markovic, who was its president. It was a party of the Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And why didn't you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. There seems to be something that -- it seems Judge Brydensholt as well, and myself as well at least, are not understanding. Just a couple of seconds ago, to the question whether he did join one of the parties, the SDS party, for example, he gave a categoric no answer. Then he says that he joined a movement for Yugoslavia, the one by Ante Markovic, and now you are asking him why did he join the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Why did he not. It should have been translated why didn't he.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is: You joined the movement for Yugoslavia, the Ante Markovic movement, but you did not choose to join the SDS. You're being asked why did you not join the SDS? Did you have a reason for not joining the SDS, as a Serb, as a Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I considered the party that I entered into, that is, the party that I became a member of, had, among its members, the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Roma, so all the entire population represented in my village, all of my schoolmates, neighbours, and workmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the members of the Chamber the name of the party you did join?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: This party had among its members representatives of all the ethnicities of the people who wanted to preserve the former country, Yugoslavia. Ante Markovic had its branch offices in all the municipalities. Skelani also had its local board that I joined, of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the name of that party the Reformist Party?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, because of the rising tensions that you've described in the Skelani area, did there come a time when Muslim men began to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in late March, early April, there was something very odd going on in the relations between the Muslims and the Serbs. In the municipality of Srebrenica, the Skelani local commune, that's where the SDA membership was in the majority. This party was arming the Muslims, that is, the Bosniaks, through the reserve police force. At the time in Skelani, in peacetime, there were some five or six police officers. When the SDA party came to power, there were some 50 Muslims forming the reserve police force at the SUP in Skelani. They wore uniforms and carried weapons, that's to say, rifles and pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did young Muslim men either join the police force or otherwise leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: There were some who joined their ranks, who were aged 20 and above, and there were those who went to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you know, if anything, what they did in the woods?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that in Skelani, where I lived, the Serbs found it very hard to live there because of the circumstances arisen with the SDA party and the reserve police force. The Serbs were frightened because they were not represented in the SUP on an equal footing. The Serb citizens did not trust the Muslims, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did any Muslim citizens at that time go across the river toward Bajina Basta, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Every day the Muslims and the Serbs went to Bajina Basta. They were commuters, because there were Muslims who worked in Bajina Basta for many, many years. Serbs too. And nobody placed any obstacles in their way of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, did a man named Besim Mandzic become prominent in a political sense?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about Besim Mandzic and what he did during this time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Besim Mandzic is my neighbour. He lived 150 to 200 metres from my house; that's where his house was. Mr. Mandzic has a degree in mechanical engineering. He graduated from a mechanical faculty in Serbia, as a -- had a scholarship from a local company where his father worked. After graduating from the university, he returned to Skelani. This is when the war broke out, and he joined the SDA party and became one of the leading members, at least as far as Skelani is concerned. And later on in Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also hear of a person named Naser Oric during this time period, around April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Had you heard of Naser Oric, or see Naser Oric, prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I used to see the gentleman in Srebrenica in a gym hall where he trained. I watched him wearing sports clothes. I also saw him in Bratunac, riding a motorcycle, also wearing sports clothing. And I saw him in a coffee bar wearing a police uniform as well, in Skelani. I saw him in a uniform on the 4th of April, 1992, in a coffee bar called Merima, which was owned by Bekir Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, before 1992, what, if any, kind of reputation did the person called Naser Oric have in the Skelani region?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Naser had quite a reputation, a positive one as far as the Muslims were concerned. He was their idol, their commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you saw him in this cafe that you've mentioned, did he have people around him or was he by himself?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, he arrived in a Golf II car that belonged to the Srebrenica SUP, in the company of the new chief of police appointed by the SDA. They entered the coffee bar. They sat at a double table. Radif, the policeman who worked in Skelani at the time, was with them in company; Mandzic Besim, another gentleman, and several reserve policemen appointed by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you remember the date that you saw Naser Oric in the cafe in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I think that it was a religious Muslim holiday. It could have been Bajram, the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the person you mentioned with him, Besim Mandzic, is this the same Besim Mandzic that you told the Trial Chamber about earlier as being involved in the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there a man named Ahmo Tihic also present at the cafe that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is a local --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: He was a local Muslim leader in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was he seated at the table with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Ahmo Tihic's profession was, or what he did during that time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmo Tihic worked at the time in Bajina Basta, in a company called Teratrans. It's a transportation company. He drove a truck. After working hours, he raised cattle -- sold cattle with his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was he ever involved in arms trading?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what you know about Mr. Tihic and his arms trading dealings, if anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmo Tihic worked in a transportation company, hauling company. He travelled through the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia and Europe. He armed the Bosniak people in Skelani. He bought weapons for them, and they had to pay for each rifle. At the time people had to sell a cow in order to buy a rifle. That's how much it cost. And they simply followed their party orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, were there other people in the cafe that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were many people in the cafe, including myself. I came to the cafe together with a neighbour, a Muslim, Zurijet Ljeskovica, nicknamed Robert, born in 1961, in the village of Lijesce. We were truly good friends; we called each other pals at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the other people who were in the cafe, what was their attitude or reaction to Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: They followed each of his movements or words with pleasure, with approval. It was heartfelt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any Bosnian Serbs, other than yourself, in the cafe that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know why there were not any other Bosnian Serbs in the cafe that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: At the time the Muslims had their cafe and the Serbs had their cafe. So if the owner was a Muslim, that establishment was frequented by the Muslims; if the owner was a Serb, then that place was visited by the Serbs. In addition to that, there was also a state-owned coffee bar frequented by everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Mr. Mandzic, Mr. Tihic, and other people that were seated at the table with Naser Oric. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber whether they were armed or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Naser wore a police uniform, and he was armed. The other people in his company, there was a policeman called Muradif, who now lives in Sarajevo, he was also armed. The reserve policemen from that police station were armed with long-barreled weapons, rather, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, during that time period, April 1992, were you working as a driver for the Skelani TO?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you work as a driver until June 1992 for the Skelani TO?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And during that time period, when you were a driver for the Skelani TO, were you an active-duty soldier?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All of the people who were in the TO -- I don't actually understand your question. What do you mean by "active duty"? I drove a car, and in that sense I was active. But I was not at the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you issued a uniform or a weapon during that time period, as a driver?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, we had to wear a uniform. There were also periods of time when I worked wearing civilian clothes, because one couldn't drive a wounded person or a corpse to Bajina Basta wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you have a commanding officer that you reported to, as a driver for the TO?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had my orders as to which routes to take when I drove the car, where to take people, and which routes to take on my way back. So yes, I received those orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in June of 1992, did you then become a driver for the civilian authorities in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And by "civilian authorities," do you mean the Crisis Staff or what evolved into the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as a driver for the civilian authorities, isn't it true that you drove both a truck and an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a driver of the ambulance, on occasion you would have to pick up dead bodies to bring them to Skelani and then transport them to Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In your capacity as a driver of an ambulance, did you have the occasion to go to the village of Ratkovici in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As an ambulance driver, did you go to the village of Ratkovici in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In June of 1992, no, not on that occasion. In 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you went to the village of Ratkovici, were you accompanied by other people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The village of Ratkovici -- well, let me tell you, I first arrived in Fakovici. I parked my car there, and together with the residents of Fakovici, I remember a policeman called Kinez who works in Srebrenica today as a policeman, and also Slavko, who owned a coffee shop, and some other 30 villagers whose names I couldn't tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you went to the village Ratkovici, had it recently come under attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In Fakovici, the people called authorities in Skelani saying that they needed an ambulance car to go to Ratkovici, the village which had been attacked by the Bosniaks, by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you went to Ratkovici in 1993, or is it your testimony, when you think about it, that you went to Ratkovici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Ratkovici, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how the village looked.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The road leading to the village is something I'm going to describe. But let me just tell you, it was horrible. The entire village was razed to the ground. There were just walls remaining. Everything had been set on fire. There were several killed animals, people. Everything had been torched, looted, and razed to the ground. One couldn't see a room intact, or an object that had not been destroyed. Everything had been looted and taken away. I helped people then. We buried corpses. I remember well that I buried an old man whose last name was Pavlovic. His son is Petko, and works today in the Zvornik MUP. I simply threw some bushes on top of him, because it was getting dark, the night was approaching, and we had to take another route on our way back so as to avoid an ambush. So we had to take a longer way home, and that was going to take more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, it was part of your job, I understand, to collect bodies. The bodies that you collected, were any of those appear to have been mutilated or scarred or otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't see what that has to do with the charges in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I think it goes at this point in time not to the credibility of this witness but to the credibility of other witness that is have testified about this attack, and the Prosecution would like to elicit corroborative evidence, if they might.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It means that the evidence of those witnesses is also irrelevant. If it's a question of corroborating on other matters, then my learned friend can go ahead. But I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we crossed that stream a long time ago at the beginning of the case, whether they were relevant or not. So I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's in the interests of saving time, obviously. We're all keen to stick to what's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's perfectly legitimate to proceed with the question. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe I asked, it was part of your job, I understand, to collect the bodies. And the bodies that you collected, did any of those appear to be scarred or mutilated or otherwise damaged?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Nobody ordered me to do that. I did that of my own free will. As for the bodies and how they were mutilated and scarred, that is something I will never forget. My job was simply to drive an ambulance car. Everything else I did was above and beyond my job, and I did it out of patriotic sentiments, of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the bodies that you collected, were they bodies of Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Those were the corpses of Serb mothers, fathers, old people, residents of the village. It's a small agricultural village. People living there were mutilated, torched. Everything was looted and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, when you say "torched," would you explain to the Trial Chamber, what do you mean by "everything was torched"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Well, what does that mean? That means that people were first shot from a firearm, a rifle, a machine-gun or something like that, so first they were shot with weapons; after that they were beaten, mutilated, and set on fire. In the houses which had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is wildly speculating about things he knows nothing about. I wonder if he could be directed to provide answers based on what he himself knows. That answer has -- bears no resemblance to anything he saw himself in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is it speculation? I can't understand. Why is it speculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's asked what he saw in terms of what he meant when he said things had been torched, and he's now given a narrative about what he imagines happened in that town. It's completely non-responsive, firstly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is your description, Mr. Gligic, of what you mean by torched based on what you know, what you saw, or is it based on your imagination? Are you imagining how things could have happened, or are you telling us in how they, indeed, happened, in trying to explain to us what you mean by "torched"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not imagining anything or inventing anything. I was an eyewitness to the plight, to the suffering of the Serbian people. I was there, I buried those people, I covered their bodies with bushes. I'm now describing what I saw, not what I thought I saw, but rather what I experienced in that village at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I had my microphone switched off. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, when you use the word "torched," do you mean that something was set afire?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: When I got there with other people, there was not a single house intact. No house had a roof on it. Everything that was wooden had burned. There were bodies in orchards, in gardens. People without arms, without legs, all inter-mixed with dead pigs, who had also been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, you were a member of the army when you did your compulsory military service in 1985. At that time were you instructed, or did you know or have knowledge prior to that, on a weapon referred to as a Zolja?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I was at school, we had a subject called all national defence. Not only I, everybody who attended secondary school. That was a mandatory subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as you studied that subject, did you become acquainted with a weapon referred to as a Zolja?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you know whether a Zolja is capable to set a house on fire or any structure on fire?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it can set a house on fire. And if there is anyone in the house, that person or persons will be destroyed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the village of Ratkovici, did you personally see any evidence that the burning or torching was caused by this arm referred to as Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In the village of Ratkovici, I couldn't tell you whether one Zolja or several of them had been fired. All I can tell you is that force was used in that village. Mr. Stevanovic, who had been killed -- I will tell you what happened to them. His genitals had been cut off and placed into his mouth. Therefore, force had been used on those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether, according to what you saw, any of the houses could have been set on fire by means other than a Zolja?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. The houses were set on fire by physical means. People were first killed, then the houses were looted, and then set afire. It was a way of intimidation, to ensure that people would not return back there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you say that the houses were looted in Ratkovici, does that mean to you that there were goods missing from the houses or the surrounding house -- surrounding the houses?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In all houses inhabited by people, there were food items and basic necessities needed for life, various objects. All of that had been collected and taken to Srebrenica, or to perhaps some other bases which were closer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, did you, during the summer of 1992, as the ambulance driver, go to other Serb villages where you witnessed similar incidents of burning or looting?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the villages Krnjic and Maljani. Two villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you explain to the Trial Chamber what you witnessed there in terms of torching or in terms of the deaths of people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The attack on the village of Maljani, which is a Serbian village with a church, took place on the 4th of July, 1992. The village was completely looted, destroyed. People who happened to be in the village were killed. We, from Skelani, could not arrive right away, because just outside of the village were Muslim lines, front lines. After some seven days, I managed to recover some bodies from Maljani and took them to the chapel in Bajina Basta. I remember that there was a corpse without a head, and we buried that corpse in a metal casket. Most of the people were buried in a metal casket because it was quite warm so as to avoid the stench. That's why we did it. In that village, a priest was also killed, and that priest had a parish in the village of Maljani. The name of the priest was Boban Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, the two villages that you mentioned, were they also burned down?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, during this same time period, and through the fall, did you visit the village of -- or did you go to the village of Bozici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Bozici and Pribojevici. These are two villages next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber why you went to those villages, and what you saw when you arrived at those villages.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All of these villages around Skelani were predominantly Serb villages. All of them had been looted, burned down, and any people who happened to be in the village were killed in the most brutal way, most brutal methods known nowadays. I took all of these corpses to the chapel in Bajina Basta, their records there reflecting in what shape those bodies were, whether they were missing a head, an arm or a leg, and so on. Mr. Stankovic, a pathologist from Belgrade, and a an inspector from the SUP in Skelani, recorded all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were those corpses that you transferred to Bajina Basta, were those Bosnian Serbs or were they Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All those corpses were Serbs. These were poor people who had nowhere to flee. They only had their homes. And they could not even imagine that such crimes would be committed against them by their own neighbours. And they had nowhere to go. We didn't have a chapel in Skelani. That's why we had to take them to Bajina Basta. And besides, Skelani only had an out-patients' clinic; it did not have a health centre, like in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you state that the villages were destroyed, were burned, would it be your testimony, similar to Ratkovici, some of the buildings had been set on fire by people, or something?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The method of attack by the Muslim population against the Serbian villages was as follows: First, the army set out killing people, followed by people who were not able-bodied for the purposes of the army who would set everything on fire, but prior to that would loot everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also have the opportunity to visit the town of Brezani during that same time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to Brezani, but I was involved in the pulling out of the corpses, because Brezani was surrounded by Muslim settlements, and whoever remained there was killed. A year later, the corpses were exhumed and given a proper burial in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I'll ask you again: Those corpses, were those the corpses of Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: They were all Serbs from Serb villages, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, in September of 1992, was the Independent Battalion established in the town of Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In early September, the TO was transformed into an independent battalion, formed in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, prior to that, did Skelani have a village guard?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber, about how many people were active in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: It all depended on the village in question. The Serbs were guarding their houses from the Muslims, because in the area of Srebrenica, the predominant population was Muslim. Of course, everybody was afraid, and the Serbs were guarding their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs participated in the village guard prior to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I can't say how many. Whoever owned a home had to have guarded it, if the person had a home, a house, and a family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, were the village guards issued uniforms or issued proper weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Do we take your previous question, or your last question, "do you know how many Serbs participated in the village guard prior to September 1992," as being a generic one, or is it -- do you mean to have it related to a particular village?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, the village guard in the area. We're talking about the Skelani area. Let me rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, because we want to make sure that he understood you that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood you that way, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, I'm referring to the area of Skelani. How many village guards participated in that area, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The predominant population in Skelani was Muslim. There were very few Serbs in Skelani, you know. I believe I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, when the independent battalion was formed in September 1992, were the members of the village guards, along with the TO, incorporated into the independent battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, more or less, how many members of the independent battalion were there in the Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The independent battalion in Skelani was formed in early September, and it had some 400 to 450 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were these men formerly in the TO and the village guard?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when the independent battalion formulated, was heavy artillery, such as tanks, anti-aircraft missiles, were they then stationed in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When the independent battalion was formed in September 1992, and then in the succeeding months - October, November - did there some a time period when heavy troop reserves from outside of the Skelani area were stationed in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: When the autonomous battalion was formed, the strategic defence of Skelani was situated on a locality called Jezero, and that's where the battalion was stationed throughout. It was deployed to this area called Jezero. Otherwise, there was no army in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So Skelani, in essence, in terms of soldier power, manpower, remained basically as it had prior to the formation of the independent or autonomous battalion; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was there a command headquarters located in Skelani for this independent battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The headquarters were housed in the building of the power supply company, some -- a dozen people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: There were a dozen people working at this command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, who was in charge, the commander, of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: For a while it was Mr. Bosko Vukovic. At a later stage it was Rajko Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there someone named Ramiz who worked at the command headquarters also?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ramiz probably worked in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you work at the command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I was a driver for the medical corps, and that's what my line of duty was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So at this time were you a driver for both the Crisis Staff or War Presidency and the independent battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: At the time I worked for the battalion, and, when need arose, I worked for the Crisis Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you continue to drive the ambulance and truck for those two organisations?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, up until the 15th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During your work career with them, between September 1992 and into the winter of 1993, did you ever drive military transport, such as APCs or tanks or things that were armed and carried weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. I only drove this Lada of Russian make, a station wagon, and a Niva, and a 10-tonne truck that was -- that had the Red Cross sign on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were you armed, as the driver of this Red Cross truck?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I had my personal sidearm, a pistol, 7.65 of the Zastava make, produced in Kragljevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, during any of your activities that you've described to us, going to the village of Brezani or Ratkovici, or Kozici, did you ever use your weapon in order to shoot or to wound or to kill someone?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. This was a personal sidearm that I had from before the war, and I carried it around for security reasons. I was driving an ambulance. I couldn't be carrying a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, I'd like to ask you about January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before you come to another point, I just wanted to know a little bit more, to clarify the relationship between the village guard and this independent battalion. You told us that Skelani at that time had about 1.200 inhabitants, and then you told us that the battalion, including the village guard, comprised about 400 to 450 men. Now, these 450 men, where did they come from? Did they come from the area around Skelani? And how many people have been -- did come from Skelani directly, who had been members of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "Skelani," I mean the following: Skelani spreads out perhaps a kilometre in perimeter, and there's Rosulje, Srpska Zabokvica, and other hamlets. All these people were guarding their homes. I know for a fact, for the people who were my neighbours, who were -- who lived nearby, and I can vouch for myself, that we all guarded our homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, the number of 400, 450, have these been members of village guards of Skelani -- centre of Skelani -- the main place of Skelani, and the hamlets? Or this number of 400, are they all the people who came from outside of your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stood guard until the establishment of the independent battalion. As soon as the independent battalion was established, people joined it and were holding positions at Jezero. And at the time there were no men in Skelani, only women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But just this so-called independent battalion, has it been composed of people from your area, or are there people coming from other places, out of Skelani, who had been part of this independent battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the people from Skelani joined the independent battalion, I mean the residents of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Madam Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, in January of 1993, would you please tell the Trial Chamber where the front lines of the Bosnian Serb army were located, and the lines for the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The Skelani Battalion was deployed in Jezero. Around Jezero there was this semicircle of the defence line formed by the Srebrenica army, I mean the Muslim units. The Muslim units stretched out from Kragljevode to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't catch the name of the other place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the place of the other -- the name of the other place, from Kragljevode to ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance between the Serb and the Muslim armies was as follows: The Skelani Battalion was deployed along Jezero and was facing the Muslim army, whereas the Muslim army stretched out from -- there's this gap between Jezero and Kragljevode, and then the Muslim army was deployed as of Kragljevode in the direction of all these Muslim villages where they knew that they could seize the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And this place that you referred to as "the gap," is there a name given to that location?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. I believe it's called Vitez. There's a hunting lodge there. This was a terrain that was under nobody's control, for security reasons. It may have only been used by one or the other side in some of the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in January of 1993, did there come a time period when reinforcements did come to Skelani to help protect Skelani, reinforcements from Jezero or from other battalions, such as Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In January, Skelani did not -- or, rather, they did receive help. After the attack on the 18th of January, there was this reinforcement in the form of a unit arriving from the corps, because, of course, the battalion in Skelani was an independent one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But before the 18th, then, of January, would it be your testimony that there was no outside help that came into Skelani with reinforced military weapons or materiel?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. There were just Serbs from Bosnia who owned houses in Bajina Basta, and then joined, of their own free will, this unit to help their people and, at the same time, to defend their homes that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to get into the attack next, but I think that we might want to take a break, and then I'll begin it in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can have the break now. We usually would have a 25-minute break and go on until 7.00. If you are interested, as I used to do in the Brdjanin case, when we were sitting in the afternoon, to reduce the break period from 25 minutes to 20, and finished at 6.30 instead of 7, then we can. But it needs the -- I mean, I know that the parties will agree, but I want to make sure that the interpreters and the technicians agree to that, which would basically mean 20-minute breaks rather than 25-minute breaks, and then we'll be able to finish at 6.30, and roughly we would have had the same sitting time. But it's up to you. I mean, you confer with the registrar -- with the registrar and let me know. Let me know. In which case we'll resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, we were speaking about January 1993. Did there come a time period when the village of Skelani was attacked?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, 1993, at 5.30 in the morning, the Muslim units launched their attack at what was then the municipality of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber what you were doing that day and what you did throughout the day, during the time period of the attack.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I attack commenced at 5.30 in the morning. My house is in the centre of Skelani, and I spent the night at home. I was sleeping in my clothes, so I jumped from my bed and went out the terrace door. I was running all the way to this low wall across from my house where the post office and the church are situated. The attack by the Muslim units against Skelani commenced at the same time against the entire perimeter of Skelani. There was fire from firearms, hand-held rocket-launchers, sub-machine-guns, and fire was opened at Skelani, lying at the very mouth of the Drina River, at the foot of a hill. The attack commenced from an elevated point on the hill from the Muslim villages, that is to say, from the Serb villages that the Muslims had already taken earlier on. The shooting was heavy up until 8.30. The intensity went down as we reached 1100 hours. At that time, above my house in the orchard Vocnjak, it is some 100, 150 metres as the crow flies, I could see there men wearing camouflage uniforms. Those were white camouflage uniforms, and green camouflage uniforms as well. They were shouting, swearing, yelling. They were shouting Allahu Akbar, we'll kill you all. The Serbs started running away in the direction of Serbia, Bajina Basta, and as they were running they were getting killed along the road. There's a bridge across which one can reach Bajina Basta, and it was on this bridge that most of the people got killed, including children. Had those gentlemen known that there were not many people in Skelani, they would have probably entered Skelani immediately and set it on fire. However, they chose not to. Around Skelani, all those Serb villages that were nearby had been set on fire, looted, and people were killed. In Skelani, on that day, 57 people were killed, and there were many wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, excuse me, I'd like to ask you a question about Bajina Basta. Did you go to Bajina Basta during the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It might have been some -- it might have been 8.00 and 20 minutes that I was driving Dimitrovic's children. One of them was hit in the head, and the other in the spine. The child that was hit in the head, I took the child to the nearby cafe, whereas the other child was driven on by my brother. I took, later on, the other wounded and dead to Bajina Basta. By 11.00, the attack stopped, and at that point I saw Muslims. These were civilians. There were horses among them. And they were taking food, cattle, and captured people with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, where did you see those Muslims that you describe as taking food, cattle, and captured people with them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: It was on the bank of the Drina, in Skelani. As you turn around, you can see that there are hills all around. The Muslims were hiding in the hills, whereas Skelani lies on the bank of the Drina River. That's why the Muslims had a good vantage point; they could see the people on the move. And the distance was quite a small one, because up above my house, and those of others, there's woods. And from there they were shooting at people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how could you, in the midst of the attack, see the Muslim people confiscating goods or carrying goods out of the homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Well, from the point where I was standing, as well as other people, it was only 150 metres behind our houses that there were there civilians, hauling cattle with them, our cattle, as well as food and everything else they had looted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did the locations where the civilians who were hauling the cattle, did they have names? Were they the names of small towns or hamlets, or did you refer to that area in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Those are places located 1 to 5 kilometres from Skelani. Rosulje, Zarkovica, Srpska Zabokvica, Kalimanici. We could see smoke rising up, indicating that the houses had been sent on fire. We could hear crying, people's voices, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the places you've just mentioned, Rosulje, Zarkovica, are these places where there were Bosnian Serb houses or Bosnian Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The villages Zarkovica, Rosulje, Kalimanici, Maltasi, are ethnically pure Serb villages. Popovici, Visoki, there's a church there. These are purely Serbian villages. And a part of Zabokvica, this is why we distinguished between the Serb Zabokvica and the Muslim Zabokvica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you saw soldiers and you saw civilians. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber whether the say whether the soldiers confiscating goods from your vantage point of the Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The soldiers fired, attacked, and killed. Some of the soldiers, together with civilians, with women and children and men who are not fit for the army, they hauled cattle with them and carried various property items and food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were horses. Were you able to see who, if anybody, was riding the horses?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. I didn't see. I couldn't recognise faces. I saw horses, but I couldn't tell you who was riding horses or leading them. I couldn't give you names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me rephrase that. Could you tell whether there were soldiers or civilians riding the horses?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did the horses have mounted on them any of the confiscated goods?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various objects, sacks, probably filled with food, mounted on the horses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified also that houses had been set on fire. Were these houses set on fire before the looting, or were these houses set on fire after the looting?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: After the looting, in order to intimidate the residents and make them leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to go up into that area that you described, those surrounding Serb houses on the hill, after the attack was over?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: After the attack, at around 1, 1.30, or perhaps 2.00, when the attack was over, and when the Muslim units withdrew into the forest and perhaps further away, we entered the villages, Rosulje, Zarkovica, and Maltasi, Kalimanici, and Serb Zarkovica. The houses, more than 90 per cent of them had been set on fire. Pigs and hogs were killed, whereas cattle was hauled away. The houses were empty; there was nothing in them. We found corpses of mutilated people. All of the corpses we found there were taken to the morgue in Bajina Basta, and the wounded were taken first to Bajina Basta and then on to Uzice and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you looked at the property that had been destroyed from close up, to your knowledge, was that property destroyed by what you phrased or termed earlier "torching," or do you think that property was destroyed during the attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The attack of the Muslim forces, Muslim units, on the Serb property during which people were killed, houses were looted physically and then set on fire, all of this was perpetrated by people, by physical means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you transport any wounded people from those areas to Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Trial Chamber the types of wounds they might have had.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All of these people were wounded from firearms, hunting weapons, automatic weapons, and other pieces. The doctors in Bajina Basta made their findings. I don't know what they concluded medically. My job was just to take the wounded to Bajina Basta, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you observed the different houses that had been destroyed, was it your belief that people could move back into those houses after that attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, isn't it true that the Bosnian Serbs who lived in those houses did not move back into the houses after the attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: To this day, in certain villages, people are still unable to return to their homes. They don't have the money to rebuild their houses. These people live in group housing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many people were killed in total in the houses up on the hill?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All I know is what happened in Skelani. Fifty people were killed, and 30 or so were wounded. In the territory of Skelani municipality, over 100 to maybe 120 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that the reinforcements from Jezero only arrived the day after the attack was over?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Jezero, where the troops were, was surrounded for some three days, perhaps two days or three days, by a Muslim unit. Somehow they managed to get out of this encirclement. I don't know how, but they managed. I know that they had been encircled, and it was impossible to get any food or any aid to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, you've testified that the bridge going over to Bajina Basta, that some people were killed going across the bridge. I'd like to ask you: Were they killed by sniper fire, or were they engaging in combat with the attacking Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: There was no combat in Skelani, there was just an attack of Muslim units against the Serbian population, the infirm. Some people tried to flee and jumped in the river. People were killed, children, women. A mother was killed and her three children. One of the kids was shot in the spine. People were killed by snipers, rifles, everything. Had the gentlemen known that there was no army in Skelani, they could have entered Skelani and killed us all. And they were just one step away from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, which gentleman are you referring to at this point in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's gentlemen, actually. It's plural. Had the gentlemen know -- I think it was a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Which gentlemen? Which gentlemen are you referring to at this point in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean, on the Serbian side or the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, you testified, "had the gentlemen known that there was no army in Skelani, they would have entered Skelani and killed us all." Which gentlemen are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I mean their people, their commander, Naser Oric, Tihic Ahmo, and the others there, other unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From having worked at the command headquarters of the Independent Battalion, were you aware of who might have been leading the army of Srebrenica, the force that you say attacked?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, he didn't talk about a unified force attacking, he talked about unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I didn't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question was "leading the army of Srebrenica," which implies there was some single force, whereas the witness was referring to unit commanders. And he's referred to Muslim units throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think he referred to Srebrenica army in the testimony at the beginning of the attack. I cannot scroll my transcript down. I can certainly rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case of rephrasing it in any case. The witness has asked -- has heard the submission by Mr. Jones, in particular, and perhaps if you either repeat the question with an addendum to what he exactly means, whether it's an ad hoc, a specific Srebrenica army, or whether it's units here and there that he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, the force you referred to, whether it be units or whether you referred to Srebrenica army, could you please tell us, after having worked at the command headquarters, who might have been in charge of those units or that army?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All of the attacks of the Muslim units in the territory of Srebrenica municipality were led by the commander, Naser Oric, and those subordinated to him, Ahmo Tihic, Zulfo Tursun, and the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, do you know a person named Beli Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was he killed in the attack on Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was Beli Salihovic a Bosnian Serb or a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Beli Salihovic was a Muslim, and he was one of the more prominent fighters under Naser Oric, because they sought him for exchange on a number of occasions, or rather his corpse, because they knew that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where he was killed in Skelani on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihovic was killed above Skelani, above the bridge. That's where the spot was. When the people in Skelani, or rather, when they started looking for our people, both the dead and alive, and as they were extinguishing fires, they found Beli Salihovic there with his sniper rifle. Nowadays, somebody in Skelani has his sniper rifle as a trophy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there other Muslim soldiers that were found in Skelani after the attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know their names, because they were not originally from the Skelani area. There was just one man from Dobrak whom I knew. He was exchanged. As for the others, both those who were dead and alive, I did not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned exchanged. Were some of the dead Muslim soldiers returned or exchanged or transferred to Muslim army units or the army of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: All of the Muslims killed in the attack, including Beli Salihovic, were exchanged, from the 23rd of January until the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you participate in those exchanges where the Muslims were turned over to the Muslim forces, or the other side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, how did you come to participate in those exchanges?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Jezero, where our troops were stationed, after the troops withdrew to Skelani, there were some casualties, Serbs in those villages who had been killed. So when I came to Jezero with my 10-tonne truck to take them to Skelani, where a large grave was being prepared to bury these people, then Zivana Trifunovic, between Kragljevode and Jezero, she covered that distance on her own, and delivered the letter to Mr. Bosko Vukovic and Rajko Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the person you referred to, Zivana Trifunovic, do you know where she was coming from when she delivered the letter?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: She came -- they brought her from Srebrenica to the demarcation line. I don't know how she got there. She just arrived there. She couldn't have arrived there on foot. They brought her to Vitez, to the free territory. She arrived there in tears; she was very much afraid. And she brought the letter with her. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Vukovic took the letter. We put her in a car. So the truck remained in Jezero. We put her in a car, in a passenger vehicle, and took her to Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether she had been held as a prisoner or not in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, she had been captured. And her daughter remained in Srebrenica as a hostage, together with other people. And then the battalion command, upon reading the letter, sent a response probably to them. I took her to Jezero, and then she went back on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you said that she was brought by some people, by "they." Did you have a chance to see how the people who brought her were dressed, or did you have a chance to meet them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I saw those people at the demarcation line in Vitez, when she was brought there with her daughter to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, after she handed over the note to the people you describe as Mr. Vukovic, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Kuljanin read the letter, and then Vukovic told me to take a radio line. We took some -- we went some 50 metres away from the headquarters, to a meadow there, and established contact with the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what type of radio equipment you were using?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Well, the equipment, that equipment, was used both by the Serbs and the Muslims. That was a typical equipment which existed in the former Yugoslavia. Every defence office in every city in Yugoslavia had that type of equipment. It was a field radio set called 12, and they also had Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you said that you made contact with the Muslims. Do you know where the communication was going to specifically?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic established contact with the Muslim side. Somebody responded on the Muslim side, most likely Mr. Besim Mandzic, the person who later became chief in Srebrenica. He introduced himself, and then they agreed on the terms of exchange. Mr. Vukovic said, "Skelani speaking. Is that the Ustasha command?" And when they called us, they said, "Is that the Chetnik command in Skelani?" This is how we knew that we had established contact. When Mr. Vukovic -- when they asked whether people could be exchanged, I volunteered for that. The first exchange was held on the 23rd of January. On that day, in a FAP truck 13, with red tarpaulin cover, I brought in several of their corpses and drove back Serbian corpses, which I received on the Muslim side. They also gave me a letter indicating terms for future cooperation. On the Muslim side, there was a man who introduced himself as Nisad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, then, that your participation in the exchanges consisted of, again, being the driver and transporting prisoners to Vitez and then transporting the exchanged persons back into Skelani. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did, and I volunteered to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that the first exchange was on the 23rd of January. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber, who was present on the Bosnian Serb side during that exchange, other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: There was no one. My superiors remained in Jezero, where the front line was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber who was on the Muslim side during that exchange on the 23rd of January?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I had personal contact with only one Muslim. And away from us, towards the forest, because this took place in the vicinity of a forest, there were other Muslims who shouted, cursed, and so on. Nobody harmed me at the time, but they cursed, they swore, and they were armed. This Muslim man helped me load the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And during that exchange on the 23rd, do you know the names of the people or the names of the deceased who you brought back?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The first exchange in which I participated, Zivana and her daughter, who were alive, were with me, plus three bodies in body bags, whose names I don't know. These are the corpses that I took to the morgue in Bajina Basta. And the command, as well as the health centre, should have further details concerning these dead people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Zivana's daughter?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I knew, but I forgot her name. She got married in the meantime. I knew her very well. I carried her in my arms. She was six or seven years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know the last name of Zivana or her daughter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he said it already. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could suggest whether the name of the girl was Svetlana.
