utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the name of the daughter was Svetlana?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't remember, it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. However, I think that you're right, that the name is right. The mother's last name is Trifunovic. The girl got married, so she has a different last name now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you transported three bodies also. Could you tell the Trial Chamber how those bodies were dressed.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the bodies at all. They were naked. No uniforms were on them. Just naked corpses in body bags. And this gentleman, Mr. Mirsad, helped me load them on the truck. They didn't give me any information about these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you have any official paperwork concerning the people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I received an envelope, sealed. There was a letter inside. And I was to deliver it to the command. It had to do with the future cooperation. What were the contents of the letter, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when there was a subsequent, another exchange of either letters or people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, was there another exchange that you participated in, either of people or of letters, documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the date of -- what was the date of the next exchange, after the one on January 23rd?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The next exchange was the exchange of letters only. Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Kuljanin received the letter from them and then sent a letter to them. It was probably a list of people captured in Srebrenica, and also information about whether an -- whether there were any living people or corpses to be exchanged. The agreement was to exchange all for all; the living and the corpses on the Serb side to be exchanged for those on the Muslim side. However, in Srebrenica, there were some people who signed an oath of loyalty to the commander of Srebrenica. They remained living in Srebrenica. I think that there was just one elderly man and woman who left alive, and the others perished without a trace. They were not even exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, was there a subsequent exchange on the 27th or 28th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll wait until the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to say, at this point, we'd prefer if my learned friend wouldn't lead the witness. Obviously there was a lot of leading on background matters, which we didn't object to. From this stage on, we'd be grateful -- we fear this witness may adopt any suggestion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair enough. In fact, Mr. Jones has been extremely indulgent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I agree. We'll let the witness testify at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, would you please tell the Trial Chamber what was the date of a subsequent exchange, if there was an exchange, after the one you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The first exchange was the Trifunovic's daughter and the three corpses. There was a total of five exchanges. Two exchanges concerned -- that is, four exchanges in all. Two exchanges concerned letters only, and two exchanges were actually exchanges of persons. I don't know why this period of 40 days had to elapse, why the people could not be exchanged earlier on. But I know that I attended five exchanges, and the last one was on the 26th. On the 27th of January, we exchanged the people captured in Kusici, Otave, Zarkovici, Maltasi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you remember on the date of that exchange of those people, who you were taking to Vitez to turn over to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I think it was a family. There was a son and a father who had been brought over to Skelani. I don't know where they hailed from. They might have been over there from Radijevici; that the Serbs had caught them, and these people were then used for the exchange. When I left Skelani, I noticed that these were not dangerous men. They were farmers who had nothing to do with the war. From our conversation, they were seated next to me, they were only handcuffed, so in our conversation they were complaining. I started out by saying, why did we need this war, we could have lived together nicely. They complained that they were forced to go and loot Serb villages. When I asked them who had forced them, they both said in one voice that it was Naser who had forced not only them but all of the civilians present in Srebrenica who could not have joined the army, for this reason or another. But they were then ordered to become looters. When I took them over to the separation line, Mr. Mandza, who was the person authorised for the exchange on the Muslim side, was very angry at the time. Why was this? Because I did not bring over his relative from Salihovici, that is to say, his relative Salihovic. And he was dissatisfied with me bringing these two men, because he apparently held those who got killed in combat in higher esteem than the ones who remained alive. Then I received another letter from Mandza which I delivered to Mr. Vukovic in Skelani, both to Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Kuljanin. They got in touch, and that's how the following exchanges ensued.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, the person that you referred to as Mandza, do you know that person's complete name?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that this man hailed from Potocari, the area there. Out of the five exchanges, he attended four of them. He wasn't there during the first exchange. He wore a camouflage uniform and a white belt. He had a hat on his head, and he was wearing a big moustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gligic, you testified that a 40-day period had elapsed on the exchange that took place on the 26th. Is it your testimony that that exchange took place on February 26th, or another date?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The last exchange was on the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The exchange after the one on the 23rd of January, when the Muslim family, the young men and the father, do you know, more or less, what date that occurred?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the date itself at present. I remember clearly the date of the first exchange and the last exchange, whereas in this period between the two, there was the 4th when there was just an exchange of letters, then the 13th of February, I'm not sure about the date though. I know that there were three exchanges of people and two exchanges of letters only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When we go to the second exchange of people, do you remember the people you exchanged from the Muslim side during that second exchange of people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I do remember. These were people from the village of Kusici, Dvizovici, Zarkovica, and perhaps another village. Those were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the names, family names or first names, of the people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I remember a child, a boy, by the family name of Mitrovic. There were Ristic, Mitrovic, Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Were there any elderly people in that exchange?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any elderly men in the exchange?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: On the Serb side, the ones brought over by the Muslims were all elderly people, women and children. And when I say "elderly people," I mean aged 65 and above.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber, if possible, the physical appearance of the Bosnian Serbs that you received from the Muslim side during that exchange.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: When they brought these people over, they were beaten up, black and blue. They were unable to walk. I was under a special order to take them to the medical centre in Bajina Basta to have them examined by a physician. There was this one young girl who had committed suicide ten days later. She had been raped and was unable to cope with the experience. She was wounded and, as such, was taken to Srebrenica. I took her over to Bajina Basta. I dressed her wounds with alcohol. She had this wound in her thigh. She refused to talk, and some ten days later, when she was released from the hospital, she committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, during that second exchange of people, the one that you've just described, could you tell us who was present on the Serb side of the exchange, other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I believe that there was Dane Katanic, on behalf of the Serbian authorities; Mr. Rajko Kuljanin, an officer; and Bosko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you know please tell the Trial Chamber who was present on the Muslim side, other than the prisoners that they turned over?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: On the Muslim side, there was Mandza, the man from Potocari, who was most probably authorised for the exchange. Ahmo Tihic. Ramiz, I don't remember his last name. I only know that before the war he worked in the military department with Mr. Vukovic. And two or three more people whose names I either don't remember or don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you exchanged the body of Beli Salihovic to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. On the 26th, that was the last exchange -- there was this one exchange of papers only, and then the last exchange scheduled on the 26th, and it was due at 100 hours, that is, 1300 hours in the afternoon. Mr. Vukovic had agreed with Ramiz and the others over the radio line over this exchange. There was a lot of snow in the area. We started up our 110 truck. We boarded Beli, and we reached Vitez. But the truck couldn't be driven onwards. I went up there, told them that I was sent there, that there was an exchange to take place. And I asked for their assistance, if I could be given some oxen to draw a cart. I got there without carrying any weapons, hardly aware of what I was doing. There was this forwarding agent who gave me two oxen and a child, whose name I don't remember. And we boarded Beli and the other corpses. There was Vukovic also. And then Mandza drew this line with a stick and said that we were not to cross the line. On their side, they were supposed to surrender Ilija Ivanovic, Zdravko Nikolic, and a police officer from a special unit in Bijeljina who was most probably captured somewhere in Cerska. I'm not aware of this. They surrendered Ilija and this other elderly man from Kravica. I believe his name was Zdravko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please -- excuse me. I wanted you to tell the Trial Chamber if you were able to observe what physical condition Ilija Ivanovic was in during that exchange.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilija Ivanovic was brought in for this fourth attempt at the exchange, because this exchange was supposed to take place earlier on but was then put off for reasons unknown to me. This man was unable to walk, had cuts from -- knife cuts on his face, was bruised, unable to walk. He was weighing some 20 to 30 kilos, perhaps, like a child. I simply had to carry him in my arms over to the truck. As this was taking place, at this point in time, there were other men on the Muslim si100de who were participating in the exchange. And some 20 metres away from them, there was a group of Muslims who were armed to their teeth, who formed a semicircle. And in the centre of the circle, there was Mr. Naser, wearing a camouflage uniform, just like the ones worn by the Americans today. He wore a black beret and an automatic rifle and a bag. He wasn't taking part in the exchange at all. He just seemed to be there with those men. As we were returning from the direction -- as we were returning, there were shots directed at me and Mr. Vukovic from the direction of Koljasi. The other Mr. Vukovic was carrying Zdravko. We were walking through the woods and they were shooting upon us. I took Ilija directly to Skelani. And the people who had been waiting there at the SUP from Bijeljina were inquiring after their comrade, colleague, from Bijeljina. And I told them that I didn't -- that this man wasn't surrendered. I was also supposed to be given a child, some 12, 13 years, who was from Kusici, where everybody had been killed. But apparently all -- some of them were taken over to Srebrenica and killed. And there's only this boy, who is today 20 years of age, he's still alive, he was caught alive and taken to Srebrenica. We were aware of this. We knew where he was supposed to be located. We were inquiring after him, wanting him to be exchanged, but we never received any information in relation to this boy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gligic. I'd like to ask you the following question: You referred to a person as Mr. Naser. Now, is the Mr. Naser who you saw on that day of the last exchange the same person who you described as having seen earlier in the cafe in April 1992, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I never had any sort of a contact with this gentleman, who was a sportsman at the time. And for our generation, he was an idol, a sports idol. I used to see him in Bratunac, in Srebrenica, in the gym hall. He was working out. And I used to see him in cafes. So I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Although one can infer the answer, he actually hasn't answered your question, so you either add on to it or I put the -- I ask the witness to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the person that you referred to as Mr. Naser, on the day of the last exchange, the same person who you've described in the cafe, now the gym, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's just that when I saw him, he was wearing a military uniform and he had a beard, which he did not have before. It was a groomed beard. And he had a beret on his head. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, did he have any form of transportation, or did you see him with any form of transportation, on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No. There was a lot of snow. And the gentleman was mounted on a horse. I remember it clearly. It was a white horse. He was surrounded by the members of his elite unit. They were all armed very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you able to see the types of weapons that they were carrying?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles, machine-guns, snipers. The usual stuff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, I just have a couple more questions. I'd like to ask you that, after you participated in this last exchange, were you ever involved in exchange of prisoners from Srebrenica army or from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And during your time period that you were involved in exchanges, would it be your testimony that the Bosnian Serb army, your commanders, were able to communicate clearly concerning the exchange with the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I can't say that. I only know that they did get in touch with the radio station 12, or PT 15. There was this radio communication and the exchange of letters. I cannot vouch for the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was any use of other types of communication equipment, such as Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd still like to ask

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you still maintain in your testimony today, that as you were prior to 1992, that you have no animosity for either group, Muslim or Serb, and that your beliefs are more that there should have been political harmony in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that many Bosniaks who returned to Skelani, I have coffee with them very often. We have to live together. There are Muslims living now in the Federation. I helped them a great deal, saved their lives. And I wish to state before this Tribunal that those who are to blame for the deaths of the Serbs and the Muslims in the municipality of Srebrenica are Muslims more than the Serbs, because the Serbs did have extremists on their side, but it was the Muslims who had more of them, more of those who were criminals. And I do stand by what I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Madam Vidovic. Now, Mr. Gligic and Madam Vidovic, I start off with the usual recommendation when both the witness and the examining counsel speak the same language: Mr. Gligic, in particular, I need to address you because Madam Vidovic is always here, while you're here in front of us today for the first time. Whatever Madam Vidovic asks you, and whatever you reply, has to be translated by the interpreters, translated into English and also translated at the same time into French. Now, it so happens that most of the time, if not always, that you speak too fast, Madam Vidovic and yourself, like other witnesses, and you don't allow an interval of time between question and answer. That creates great problems for the interpreters, who will not be then in a position to catch up with either Madam Vidovic or with you. So what I kindly ask you, both of you, is to allow a very short interval of time between questions and answers, which will give the interpreters time to translate your interventions. I would also ask both of you to speak slowly, in other words, not to rush, not to speak very fast, because again, that creates a lot of problems for the interpreters, and the interpreters, after the three Judges, have probably got the most difficult work in this Tribunal. So please try to cooperate. Madam Vidovic, whenever it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gligic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to April 1992, Skelani formed part -- were a municipality with a predominant Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance. Could you please place on the ELMO an extract from the census in Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 1991, and produced by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, I mean just for the future, if it is possible that at the beginning of each testimony of each witness - Ms. Sellers, I mean just convey this to Mr. Wubben, we were thinking - I think it would help us a lot to have a standard map that is available. It is not necessarily the map that the witness will mark, put markings upon. But if we have a map at our convenience at all times, I think it would help us a lot. Because sometimes it's locating -- locating small individual places, having recourse to our memory, is not that easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had at one time prepared a rather large map that we had in the courtroom one day, and we didn't know whether we wanted to leave the map here, have Your Honours be able to take the map back to chambers. Certainly Defence counsel has seen that; they could look at it. Or to have the maps that open up that are rather large and grey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we should have a practical approach to this. One witness will probably be concentrating on one small area, another witness may be concentrating on another area which is quite a few miles away, so what I suggest is that you come prepared with each new witness with a proper map that we can follow, even if the witness is not going to be asked to put any markings on it. But it gives us an idea, more or less, of -- again, as we go along, moving from one witness to the other, how we are supposed to also move along the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? Thanks. I know that it shouldn't be that difficult for you. You can do something about it. Yes, Madam Vidovic. You are now asked to look at this document. Could you refer the witness straightaway to the part that you need him to look at, Madam Vidovic. Which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please turn to page3. In the bottom it says 230, page 230. Look at line 2 where it says "Skelani". And this is -- this relates to the census carried out in 1971. Then turn the page and look at page 231, where you have the census results dating from 1991. Look at line 2, under total, it says "1.123 inhabitants, 950 Muslims, 160 Serbs, 7 Yugoslavs, and 6" under the column "others." It is true, is it not, that in the territory of Skelani, in 1991, there were more than 900 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: That's not true. I can enumerate all the villages and places in Skelani, because I lived there, all the Muslim and Serb villages in the territory of the municipality of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, claim that the census that was officially carried out by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not true.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: It's not true, because this is not -- these are not the accurate census results. This is a political overview.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to turn your attention to the fact that I deliberately used the census results published by the Croatian State Bureau of Statistics. But I will go on with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in addition to the fact that the majority was constituted by the Muslims on the 13th of April 1992, so despite of that fact, on the 13th of April, 1992, the Serb municipality of Skelani was proclaimed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: You repeated once again that the Muslims had a majority, which is not true. Then you gave a date of the 13th of April, 1992, and that date is not correct either. It happened earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. So in the local commune of Skelani, Srebrenica municipality, the majority population was Serb population. There was a decision adopted by the Serb parliament in Pale to establish Skelani municipality, because the Serbs could not stand the Srebrenica authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it is true that that was the decision taken by the SDS in Pale and not the decision taken by the Serb residents in that area.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true. The Serb people wanted equality in the municipality of Srebrenica, and they could not gain it by any other means. They wanted to have their own judiciary organs, their own doctors, their own executive, their own policemen. They didn't want only Bosniaks to hold those posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to remind you what I told you barely two or three minutes ago. Please, you're moving too fast and you're not allowing an interval of time between question and answer and question again, all right? You're just firing questions and answers as if you are still fighting in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia. Now, let's -- Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, may I just ask you, because I have difficulties to understand these statistics. In the English version, you have numbers on the left side, and it starts "and Herzegovina based on census" and on the right side, "permanent population of Croatia originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, I'm sorry, but I just can't -- don't understand the whole thing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the title of the page is "population of Bosnia-Herzegovina national structure," or composition, "in settlements." Then on page 266, and I believe it's the same for the English version, it says that the permanent -- it says "permanent population of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the population of Croatia originally hailing from Bosnia and Herzegovina." So what you have on page 3 is just a continuation of the heading which begins on the previous page. So please take a look at page 230, where it says "permanent population of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and then the heading continues on to the following page, where it says "permanent population of Croatia originally hailing from Bosnia and Herzegovina, classified by settlements." So if you put those two sheets next to each other, you will have your answer to your question. This created some confusion for me as well, that's why I asked for an explanation. Your Honours, I would like you to instruct the witness that he must answer my questions without further elaborating or giving answers that are too broad and that I did not ask for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, madam, but you cannot convince me that something that is not true is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But you just answer the question. I will not allow you to enter into a confrontation with Madam Vidovic, because you are not here to do that. You are here to answer questions. If you don't agree with what is being suggested to you, just say, "I don't agree," and explain why. It's as simple as that. And address me and never Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I turn to my next question, I would like to tender this exhibit that I used into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need your help here, registrar. This is D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 173? Are you sure? Okay. So this document is being tendered and received as a Defence exhibit, being marked accordingly as Exhibit D173.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask the usher to put a map of Skelani on the ELMO. This is an excerpt from a larger map of the former military institute of the former SFRY. The map is from 1971, and it's an area of Zvornik 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to take a look at the map first, especially the locations which we have marked. Please take a pointer. Try to find Skelani, please. It is marked in yellow, circled with yellow. Please show that.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look to the left. Please find Jezero, which you have mentioned. It is also circled in yellow. Can you find Jezero?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. Now please show us the village of Resagici, which is marked below Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Resagici. Witness, please show Skelani, and then follow the Drina River down. Yes, thank you, you've found it.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please show us Zabokvica, which you've also mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now please show Dobrak, which you have also mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please show us Zgunja.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us Barakovici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Gornji and Donji Peci?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Poljak?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then Bukovik?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then after that, Stublovi?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sulice?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Knezovi?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also the area above Jezero. In that area, please show us Trubari?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Radovcici?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tokoljak?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now please show us the village of Tihici.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then Donji and Gornji Daliegosta above Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to ask the witness to put his initials next to these villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please put your initials in the circle around Skelani, Jezero.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also please put your initials on Trubari, Radovcici, and that would be enough.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the Trial Chamber consider that the witness has agreed that the Defence has marked those places on the map, and that is what it says on the map, but the witness certainly has not found those places on the map and marked them himself during the testimony. Now, we do have the majority of maps at this point coming in via the Prosecution witnesses. It certainly allows us to understand that that was a process in which the map was marked, and that we could not say that that would be the same for this process. If the Defence wants to elicit that there are places and that he agrees, then I think a possible other solution just might be to have it initial in the corner of the map. But he certainly didn't mark this map up. This is a map that's a Defence exhibit, it's a the creation of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is clear, Your Honours. However, I stated very clearly that it was us who marked all of these places that the witness has shown to us, and I'm sure that this is in the transcript. However, I do not object to this solution proposed by the Prosecution either. What is important to us is to ensure that all participating in this trial know about the places that this witness has mentioned, the places that we will mention, and especially that some places, such as Radovcici and Trubari be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it needs to be initialed in the places you mentioned, but if you insist, I will ask him to initial them. What I would like the witness to confirm is the following: Mr. Gligic, you have been shown -- you have seen this map. You have also seen the various places that have been highlighted on this map. You have been asked to go through these various places one by one, and you have indicated them, where they are. Do you agree that this would, in your opinion, be a good topological description of the location of these places? Or is there something wrong with this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that this map is accurate. What I do not agree with is that certain places have been mentioned by madam, such as Zgunja, for example. It is not an ethnically pure village. This goes for some other villages as well. Zgunja, Resagici, these are not Muslim villages, these are villages with mixed population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. That is not in issue at the time being. What is in issue for the time being is whether you agree whether you would accept this map as an accurate map, in other words, an accurate topographical description of the places. That's all for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we give it an exhibit number. This will be D174. Okay, thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you will agree with me that, in all of these villages, before April 1992, Muslims lived and constituted majority in some of these places, whereas in other places they lived together with Serb residents.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Partially. There were some villages among those which you have marked where Serbs constituted majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: You will agree with me, won't you, that Muslims lived in these villages and were either majority or minority.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Well, when you phrase it like that, then yes, I will agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Skelani is located on the very border with Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bosniaks, Muslims, lived in the hilly area of Skelani; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to respond to that. Perhaps 70 per cent of them did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the valley area, in the flatland area, next to the road in Skelani, Bosniak houses and Serb houses were mixed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: In certain parts, yes, and in certain parts, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your settlement of Gligici was located across from the police station in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can have a break now, and I can continue my cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So we will have just a mere 20-minute break. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I resume my cross-examination, I would like you to understand that I have come here to perform my duties and I do not have much to do with the conflict. I do hail from a mixed family. I've come here to defend my client, and it is far from my intention to pick fights with the witnesses, to discuss issues with them. I've been in situations here when witnesses were swearing at me, but I did not react to that, nor did I inform you of this. And I wish to assure you that I do not wish to enter into any sort of conflict with the witnesses here. It may simply be my style of examining. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not allow you or, for that matter, any witness to enter into such confrontation. In any case, you can rest assured that I will protect you, Madam Vidovic, as much as I will protect witnesses, although I don't think that I have had the occasion to do that so far. But you can rest on my cooperation and that of the other two Judges for sure, when it comes to that. So we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Gligic, was the following: Your house was across from the police station in Skelani, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that area. Not really across from my house, but maybe some 50 metres below. My house is across from the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, your mother worked in the elementary school in Skelani, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You lived together with your mother and your twin brother, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, in fact, ever since the establishment of the Crisis Staff in Skelani, you worked in the staff; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew precisely what was going on in Skelani and the surrounding area in April and May 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I was partly aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were even aware of the incidents taking place 30 kilometres away from Skelani. You talked about these events to the representatives from the OTP in your statement dating from 2000. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which incident you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, sir. The SDS Crisis Staff was in control of the events on the ground; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: You had the TO, the military section and the civilian section.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Different information was gathered at the SDS Crisis Staff; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Crisis Staff included the representatives of the police, the army, the health authorities, the newly established municipal authorities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I've already told you, you have the military section of the then-TO and the civilian part, the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew the people who were involved in this civilian Crisis Staff. You termed it "civilian Crisis Staff." Who were members of the Crisis Staff? You used to work for it.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Initially, I worked in the military section, and only later was I transferred to the civilian part.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will turn your attention to the statement you gave to the OTP in 2000. Do you recall giving a statement to the investigators of the OTP in 2000?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the time, and I can show it to you if you want me to, on page 03063353, that's the Prosecutor's numbering of the Bosnian version, you said that: "Because of all these events, the local Serbs established their Crisis Staff in Skelani. It was established in late April or on the 1st of May." And you said: "Since I was not married at the time, I did not have any family obligations, and I volunteered to be the driver of one of the two ambulances belonging to the Crisis Staff." And you then went on to describe the Crisis Staff. Therefore, you worked in the Crisis Staff, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: At that time I was driving the ambulance for the military section. Later on, I started working for the civilian part of it, that is, the Crisis Staff. So there's this period when I was working for the medical corps, driving the ambulance, and later on, in 1993, I was driving the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Gligic, to you is as follows: Who were the members of the Crisis Staff? Skelani was a small settlement where you resided, and I'm referring to the civilian part of it.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: You mean their names?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic; Dane Katanic; Milosevic, also known as Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that a representative of the police was also a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were close to Marko Milovanovic and Milenko Canic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I was not very close with Canic; he was a neighbour of mine, whereas Mr. Milovanovic, who was killed on the 16th of January, was a distant relative of mine, and we were in touch.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Marko Milovanovic. It is true, isn't it, that he was the commander of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: It's not Milovanovic but Milanic. He worked at the SUP before the war, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gligic. Therefore, Mr. Milanovic was the commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Skelani? And that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic was a member in charge of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Skelani at the time? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: At the time the army had its own representatives, the police had its own representatives, and the civilian authorities had their own. I believe that Mr. Mitrovic and Blagomir Jovanovic were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had direct connections with the authorities at Pale; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which period you're referring to. Can you give me a date?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period ever since its establishment in April/May 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: At the time I was driving an ambulance for the TO, therefore, for the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I again turn your attention to the statement you gave to the Prosecutor in 2000, page 6, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S version, which is page 5, last paragraph of the English version. You stated: "The Crisis Staff was in touch with the authorities in Pale over telephone lines connected to the Serbian network. I was a driver, but I believe that they were in touch with the civilian authorities," and so on.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying this. I'm just saying that I don't know which period we're talking about. Which dates are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I put to you that the Crisis Staff, ever since its establishment, was in touch with the SDS head office in Pale.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The political and civilian authorities probably had contacts with the civilian authorities in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that Dr. Radovan Karadzic's seat was located in Pale, together with the core leadership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've never heard of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I have heard this from the media, but I myself am not privy to this. I was driving an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had direct contacts with the neighbouring Serb villages; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now turn to a different matter. Today, you've described to us how the war broke out. You said that the reason or the cause was the establishment of the SDS party. However, in -- of the SDA party. However, in your statement to the Prosecutor, you provided many more details, and you said that the war in Skelani broke out on the 9th of May, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: When you say "the war," I meant the first victims, the first persons who were killed. That's what I called the war. What I mean by when I say "the war broke out," I mean the moment when people started getting killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You relate to us two incidents which, in your words, caused the war to break out, and I will get back to these two incidents later. You said that one of them occurred in Kragljevode, which is 14 kilometres away from Skelani, and the second one in Jadar, which is 30 kilometres away from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, is it really your testimony that the war broke out on account of these events?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: The cause of the war in the area of the municipality of Srebrenica and the former municipality of Skelani was the killing of the people, as well as other political events taking place there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, the truth is that the war started with the establishment, with the proclamation, of the Serb municipality of Skelani; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance, please. Could you put the following document on the ELMO: It starts with the following number: 00316884, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence. The document was issued in Sarajevo on the 13th of April, 1999, and it's a bulletin on the events in the territory of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as at the 13th of April, 1992. Could the following page please be placed on the ELMO: 00316885.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3, relating to Skelani. It reads here, and I quote: "A Serb municipality was proclaimed in the settlement of Skelani. The armed groups of Serb extremists, some of whom had crossed over from Serbia, seized all the facilities in this local commune. A portion of the population who had remained there were being mistreated. People's property is being destroyed, houses are being blown up, as well as facilities, houses, buildings, and vehicles." In relation to this, I wish to ask you the following: It is true, is it not, that on that day, the 13th of April, 1992, volunteers from Serbia were already present in Skelani and were mistreating the remaining Muslim population, destroying properties and looting.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, the Muslims who lived in Skelani, and I can give you their first names and last names, names of the people who lived there, were not harassed or mistreated. They were not harmed by anyone. The conflict started when a man from Kalimanici was killed, Danilo Petrovic, in fact. Husband, wife, and then somebody else's wife, I think their last name was Simic, were killed in Jadar. This is when the tensions escalated and the war broke out. In Skelani at the time, Ismet Hajdarevic lived with his wife --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will put questions to you about certain Muslims. However, now I asked you about something else.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: What are you asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that on the 13th of April in Skelani terror and intimidation aimed against Muslim populations started; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like this to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, might I make one comment prior to that and it's just for the sake -- we don't have the translation. It appears to me, and I'm not a speaker of B/C/S, that's -- it's a bulletin, or is this a newspaper article, as I thought I understood learned counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you furnished it to the Defence yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe that she -- it was characterised as a newspaper article, and I just want to clarify that it might be more of a bulletin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you. Bilten is bulletin, I suppose, and bulletin is even more than a newsletter. It's translated as -- I don't know. I haven't seen the original document, obviously, and this is only part of it. So I don't even know how big or how small it is, what it covers, what it doesn't cover, so I can't help you much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will explain. This is an official document issued by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 13th of April, 1992. The word used in our language is "bilten." In Serbo-Croatian, that denotes an official document. I don't know how that was translated, but I used the word in our language "bilten". This document contains excerpts pertaining to developments, events, in various places. I used only the bit pertaining to Skelani for the simple reason that I received this document quite late. I think that the Prosecution has this document. In fact, I think that we got it from the OTP. And if requested, we can send it for official translation. But all we need is this bit pertaining to Skelani. And it would be very labourious if we were to translate the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the whole question is a very simple one. What's the correct translation of the word "bilten"? I don't know because I'm an expert on the language. To me -- there seems to be the indication that "bilten" means bulletin. But I can't confirm that. I don't know. Perhaps those who are experts in the language can help us there. On the document itself it says "newsletter," but I don't know if newsletter is correct representation of the word "bilten.".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, our suggestion would be bulletin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My point, then, would be that this is a bulletin, and in terms of we're not objecting to its admission; we're just saying this comes from a governmental source, a Bosnia-Herzegovina source. It's a bulletin, not a news article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We can move ahead. The number, this will be 175, D175. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, therefore, I suggest to you that the intimidation and terror which commenced on the 13th of April, the 12th and the 13th of April, 1992, were the reason that caused Muslims to flee into neighbouring woods and more distant Muslim settlements; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I also put to you that what you stated today is not true; namely, when you said that the Muslims went from their homes into the woods in order to join other men who were fighting against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: I claim the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In reality, they were forced to flee for their lives. They left Skelani in order to save their lives and to avoid being killed.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: At the time the Muslims lived in Skelani. When the conflict started, when people started being killed, people, the Muslims, from the area, and I mean men fit for military service, went to the woods, whereas women and children transferred to Bajina Basta, to the local Red Cross. I can assure you of that, because I helped many of those who wanted to live. The men who were fit for military service went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that, in the woods surrounding Skelani, one couldn't find entire Muslim families who had fled Skelani and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: There might have been some, but most of the women and children went to Serbia, to Bajina Basta, whereas the men fit for military service went to Srebrenica and the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that Serbia and its Red Cross took those people in?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO a photograph. This is a photograph of Mr. Milos Cvetkovic from the book of "Chuck Sudetic," "Blood and Revenge," from page 194, published in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, please take a look at this photograph. This man has a cockade on his head, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, did you see sights similar to this one in May of 1992, in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask that this photograph be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, which consists on the front pages of the book "Blood and Vengeance," published by Penguin Books, and what appears to be a photograph of three person carrying arms and weapons with the inscription, "Serb irregulars, or Chetniks, on patrol during the operation to expel Muslim inhabitants of the Skelani area in May 1992 (Milos Cvetkovic)" is being admitted in evidence as a Defence exhibit, and being marked in evidence as Defence Exhibit D176. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, we don't object to the admission. It's just unclear from looking at the picture and what's written underneath whether what is written underneath is attributed to either to Chuck Sudetic or to the person Milos Cvetkovic, or is that the photographer. I think the document doesn't completely speak for itself for the origin. The Prosecution just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if Ms. Vidovic can help you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the photograph was made, as far as I understand, by Milos Cvetkovic. The comment was probably written by the author, but I cannot affirm that. I was interested in the photograph, so this is why I put a question to the witness pertaining to the photograph. In addition, Your Honours, the author of this book works for the OTP, so perhaps they could obtain the information, because the author of this book is Mr. Chuck Sudetic. May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. You have five or six minutes more. So stop whenever it's convenient for you. If you need -- it's up to you, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gligic, is it your testimony that you personally did not see anything relating to the destruction of the Muslim property?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC
utterances.text: No, I do not claim that. There were occasional excesses, but on an occasional, individual basis. This was not done by local residents, this was most likely done by other people, such as volunteers who had arrived in Skelani to defend the place for patriotic reasons. Yes, that's true, there were mistreatments, but to a much lesser extent than mistreatments of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to finish with my cross-examination for today at this point, because I have a series of other questions which I would like to embark upon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Vidovic, do you think you will finish with this witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And roughly how much time do you think you require? I'm asking you not to bind you in any way, but to give an indication to the Prosecution what time to bring the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I will need about two hours. We have a videotape that we will show. It runs for 12 minutes. So I will need two hours, two hours and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I would suggest to you, if it's two hours, two hours and a quarter, I would suggest you will have the witness ready here about the time of the first break, with the understanding that it will not be immediately after the first break that we will start with him but maybe half an hour -- half an hour after, or three-quarters of an hour later. It's up to you. But more or less, you should be put on notice now that you will be required to start with the next witness at some time during the second session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke with my co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, who is in the midst of proofing that witness. I informed him that the direct examination, the cross-examination, might end prior to tomorrow's complete session, and I understand that he feels that the proofing probably will take today and tomorrow. But he wanted me to assure the Trial Chamber that we will be on schedule with this witness, even given the earlier schedule for Thursday, that this witness will finish by the end of the week, as foreseen. So I will certainly go back and discuss this with him, but I might have to inform you tomorrow that he would prefer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tell Mr. Di Fazio to do his utmost to finish the briefing today so that we can start with the next witness tomorrow, because, I mean, it's -- and I think the next witness is going to be here for quite a long time. Anyway, Mr. Gligic, that's all for today. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. You will go back to the hotel. I'm sure that you are being well looked after. And may I please draw your attention to something very important: That between today and tomorrow, between now and tomorrow when you resume your testimony, you're not to contact anyone or speak to anyone in relation to what you are testifying about. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can adjourn now and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's one matter, but perhaps in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just very shortly, and I don't want to preempt the Prosecution on this matter. But concerning the expert report, the 94 bis motion and the response which we filed, it's just to put Your Honours on notice, really, that there may be room for agreement between us and my learned friend on the Prosecution side. And as I say, it may be that the Prosecution will file a reply, or there may be another filing on our part. But just in brief, as I say, there may be scope for an agreement along the lines that if the report could be filed without the witness attending and with the observations which we've made about the report and about the points which we wish to take being on the record. In paragraph 4 of our response, we took various points about the credibility of Dr. Stankovic, and it may be that those remarks don't need to remain if an agreement of that nature is agreed at. In other words, in fact, in our response, those observations about credibility were premised on Dr. Stankovic attending. And so if he doesn't attend, if his report goes in -- as I say, I don't want to say we've reached an agreement, but it was just to put Your Honours on notice that there may be an agreement. So you can bear it in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's a positive revelation or development. I leave it entirely in your hands. And if you can return with better news, we would gladly --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's a work in progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. It's an area where you can easily reach an agreement, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thought I should just mention it also so that Your Honours didn't render a decision on it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That helps, of course. Because this morning, when I found it on my desk, I already started -- I gave instructions to our staff to start breaking it into pieces so we can then discuss it in a logical manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps we can spare your staff some work, which might also be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All these will be appreciated, Mr. Jones, I can assure you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
